author: MSchwaibold
text:
A German tweeting about grids … oh well here goes nothing: 

Every component here follows a very simple and layered grid structure. 

First 8px base grid. I set that up as tightly as possible to allow for max flexibility later. 24px radius + Inset 24px

Second padding (safe space) and content areas showing how things are grouped together. 

Then the structure with text hierarchy, image placeholders and controls, followed by the actual font sizes and weights used in each component.

I’m only using two font families (Inter and Baskerville) and a max of three font weights and sizes per component (very important for visual hierarchy) 

Those are the basics but those constraints will get you pretty far and LLM is good at maintaining those consistently as it builds out more components on the fly.

Just sharing a glimpse of what the modern design process looks like. A dedicated app built with Toolcraft specifically for creating that carousel with a WebGL distortion effect. Not in Figma, not in Photoshop or After Effects. Completely tailored software built with Grok 4.6 to nail just one effect and make it easy to bring to live website. Not one-shotted. It took a day and plenty of iterations to explore the right math, find the right references, and lock in the right on-brand vibe.

Don’t tell me it’s not design just because we used AI. It is design - and it’s much more fun than sitting in the tool you’re afraid to leave because you feel comfortable there.

Quick thought on Grok 4.6 - super fast compared to anything else out there. Good creativity and understanding of the problem. Much, much cheaper than Fable. Fable, however, is still the best at understanding design requests. Kimi is in second place, but super slow.

author: heynavtoor
text:
Apple's product pages have that scroll effect. The camera flies through a 3D world. Products float. Scenes transition. No cuts. One continuous flight driven by your scroll wheel.

Here is what one costs to build in 2026.

Big storytelling agencies (Noomo, WithLore, Utsubo): $15,000 to $100,000. Three to six months. A team of designers, 3D artists, and WebGL developers.

Awwwards-tier flagship from a senior freelancer: $8,000 minimum.

Three.js multi-scene site with GSAP scroll: $3,500 to $8,000.

That is if you can find a Three.js specialist. They charge $75 to $150 an hour. There are fewer of them than there are brands that want the site.

Now meet scroll-world.

A free, open-source agent skill for Claude Code and Codex that generates the entire thing from a prompt.

Describe your brand. Describe the scenes. "A coffee brand. Start outside the farm. Fly into the roasting facility. Pass through the packaging. Land in the cafe."

It generates the isometric stills. It generates the camera flights. It generates the connector clips between scenes from the actual boundary frames of both neighbors, so every seam is pixel-identical. No flicker. No cut. One continuous flight.

Then it wires the chain into a portable vanilla JS scroll engine that drops into plain HTML, Next.js, or Vue.

One prompt. Hours. Not months.

6,096 stars on GitHub in 25 days. 724 forks. MIT license. Built by cyw, founder and CTO of Hermai AI, out of San Francisco.

Here is what scroll-world does:

- Interviews you on brand, scenes, art direction, and budget before spending a cent
- Generates the isometric stills through GPT Image 2
- Generates the camera flights through Seedance on Monid
- Renders a native 9:16 portrait chain for mobile, not a crop
- Ships a vanilla JS scrub engine with blob-seek, lazy load, and seam crossfade
- Installs into Claude Code as a plugin or Codex through the Vercel skills CLI
- Framework-agnostic

Here is what scroll-world costs to install:

Zero. Forever.

Generation burns credits. A 6-scene 1080p chain on Monid pay-per-clip lands around $27, printed before the run starts.

Big storytelling agency: $15,000 to $100,000. scroll-world: $27.
Awwwards WebGL flagship: $8,000. scroll-world: $27.
Three.js contractor for a month: $12,000. scroll-world: this afternoon.

Your brand. Your world. Your scroll.

100% Open Source. (Link in the comments)

title: Here is the prompt to create a liquid gold nav bar :)  Have fun experimenting!  …
author: LexnLin
text:
Here is the prompt to create a liquid gold nav bar :)

Have fun experimenting!

Create a floating navigation toolbar centered on screen. Dark background, glassmorphism toolbar with blur and subtle border.

Core feature - Golden active indicator ring: A sliding highlight around the active button built with 4 CSS layers:

Glow - blurred warm gold (#e8af48) behind the ring, opacity: 0.15
Clip container - overflow: hidden, border-radius: 18px - this clips the gradient
Rotating conic-gradient - sized 200% and offset -50% so it spins from center. Rotates 4.5s linear infinite. The gradient must be heavily gold-dominant:70% of the gradient = gold tones (#533517 dark bronze → #c49746 warm gold → #feeaa5 light gold)
2 narrow white hotspots (#ffffff, each only ~3% wide) simulating studio light reflections
Between each white hotspot, a very thin (~1.5% each) hint of #ffc0cb pink and - blue for subtle chromatic iridescence - these must stay minimal, the ring should read as GOLD not rainbow
The pattern repeats twice across 360° for symmetry

Inner plate - inset: 2px covers the center, only 2px of spinning gold ring visible. Background matches toolbar.
The indicator slides between buttons with bouncy overshoot easing (cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.2, 0.64, 1)).
3 nav buttons (Home, Search, User) with thin stroke  icons, separated by subtle dividers. Plus a dark/light theme toggle - sun/moon icons crossfade with rotate+scale. On toggle click, the button bounces up to 1.25× scale then springs back. Add film grain noise overlay and radial ambient glow.

title: Save this for the next time your typography feels weird and you can’t explain wh…
author: 0xCharlota
text:
Save this for the next time your typography feels weird and you can’t explain why.

Nine times out of ten, it’s line-height - the vertical space between lines of text that decides whether type feels confident or clumsy, readable or tiring.

Headlines
Compress them.
~1.05–1.25 is usually right.

Headlines aren’t meant to be read carefully line by line. They’re meant to land as a shape. Tighter leading pulls words into a single visual block and makes the headline feel confident and intentional.

One hard rule: ascenders and descenders should never touch. If your t’s and l’s are colliding with g’s and y’s, you’ve gone too far.

Body text
Do the opposite. Give it air.
~1.4–1.7, depending on the typeface, its x-height, and the line length.

Body text is about endurance. Your reader shouldn’t notice the typography at all. If they’re aware of the type, something’s off. The goal is that they just keep going, paragraph after paragraph, without friction.

In @framer, you can find the Line-height settings in the Text Panel > Line.

And yes, this applies even if you’re using the same font for headlines and body text!
Same font, same page, but they have completely different jobs - and different line height.

Sometimes, choosing a good type isn’t enough - you need to know how much space to give letters so they can do their work.

title: I've been using a 5-color system recently and it's the best way I know to build …
author: AlexTudun
text:
I've been using a 5-color system recently and it's the best way I know to build flexibility into a brand's pallete without things falling apart.

Here's how it works: two main colors that can swap roles. One can be the background, the other can sit on top, and you don't lose contrast or readability. I test them against each other early because brands need to switch things up - social posts, billboards, whatever - and the colors have to hold up when you flip them.

Then three accent colors. I use white or light neutrals when I can because they work on almost anything. The other two I pick based on temperature. Does this orange pop on the dark blue? Does this purple work on the neon green? The idea is different colors do different jobs depending on what's behind them. Most of the time I make sure all three accents read clearly on both main colors, but I'll bend that if the design needs it.

When a project needs more colors - heavy digital stuff, campaigns with a ton of assets - I build out from the original five. Same thinking. Same contrast checks. Just more range.

I got this from a brand guideline I saw last year. Can't remember which one. But the logic stuck. You pick colors that work together across contexts, not just in a vacuum. You don't add a color because it looks nice. You add it because it earns its place by being useful.

If you're stuck on color for a brand, try this. Start with two that can trade places without breaking. Build three accents that actually pull their weight. Hope someone finds this useful!

author: brian_lovin
text:
One way I think about this is: 

You get a certain amount of "credits" to spend to create visual hierarchy. Size, color, space, weight, typeface, etc.

The goal is to create a clear design while spending as few credits as possible.

Some designs over-spend and things feel messy.

Some designs under-spend and there's not enough hierarchy to latch onto.

A good practice is to start by spending a single credit, see how it feels, and only spend more if it's not clear yet. 

For example, if you are trying to create visual hierarchy between two pieces of text, try changing only the weight instead of changing both the weight and size at the same time.

text:
After half a decade of creating templates for the @webflow marketplace, I'm incredibly grateful for this program, which has allowed me to support my family and pursue my dream job for a significant part of my career.

I've seen many companies using my templates to speed up their development process. My work has inspired some designers and I've got good and loyal clients.

However, not sure why, the marketplace team has suddenly delisted all my main templates, which has decreased my monthly income by 80%.

It was a shock. I remain confused about the reason, as I have been a strong supporter of the company since day one, which has given me many negative thoughts, feelings of disappointment, frustration, and anger. I stopped creating templates for them for a while.

In the meantime, I created my own marketplace and learn something powerful: If something can go wrong, everything will go wrong. Lost clients, no money, no team, no income, but nothing to lose, since I've lost almost everything already.

Even so, I managed to launch an honest MVP, and after reviewing all my templates, those that were living in a limbo, I've decided to offer full access at a huge discount.

Now, anyone can get everything I've created all at once, from the top sellers to my favorite out-of-the-box templates. Buy once, build forever.

I'm back to Webflow and the Framer templates. Stronger than never.

We built this onboarding flow in React Native that feels better than most native apps
 
Here’s how we did it:

① Patched react-native-screens for a custom transition
② Button and stepper are rendered on top of the stack
③ Synced button state across screens via context

The button and header are positioned absolutely above the stack. When a screen focuses, it updates the shared button state (text, disabled state) via context

The hardest part is keeping the keyboard open during screen transitions. We solved it with hidden TextInputs that get focused programmatically before navigating

The result: one button flows across every screen and surfs the keyboard
